items.title: vllm v0.34.0
items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 To keep the old sizing, pass --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR

MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

Improvement Hardware Gain PR
Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen 4×GB200 up to 1.95× decode #65152
GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE NVIDIA 1.6× output throughput vs DEP4 #60895
Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) GB300 1.5× single-stream decode #64077
Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) GB200 GLM-5.3 TTFT 1.24–1.40× faster at 32K–128K #63956
KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) GB300 1.34–1.59× decode attention #63638
Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) NVIDIA 3.0–8.8% lower decode ITL #51012
FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark 8×MI355X +35–57% interactivity at conc. 1–8 #63440

AMD ROCm

  • Release images and wheels are ROCm 10.0 only (#61939).
  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

Install

Python wheels

Platform Install
CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) pip install vllm
CUDA 13.0 (uv) uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto
ROCm 10.0 pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100
XPU uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match

Docker images

Platform Image Short alias
CUDA 13.0 (default) vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0
CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa
ROCm 10.0 vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm

latest tags work the same way (e.g. vllm/vllm:latest-rocm). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The -efa image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576).

The Assets section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels.

Full changelog

Model support
  • Mistral Large 4 (#64534) runs on MRV2 with:
    • sparse MLA plus the DSA indexer, and cross-layer KV sharing;
    • DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse.
  • Other new models:
    • MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (#64111), plus P/D across different prefill and decode TP (#64475).
    • Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe with MTP and DFlash2 (#64282, #64944).
  • DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1
    • Prefill gathers compressed KV once per KV-source group: 38 → 4 gathers per step (#59131).
    • Decoder replay graphs share the model graph pool: prefill graph memory 15.52 → 9.88 GiB per rank on GB200 (#63155).
    • fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540).
    • DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996).
    • Engram host tables shared across DP ranks (#62359).
    • DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits on the FP8 indexer cache (#62011).
    • Packed multi-image vision encoding, 1.6–2.6× (#65030).
    • LoRA on the language model, compressor and wo_a layers (#57245, #64880).
    • DSpark with PCP (#61994); PCP with PP or DP (#63098).
    • Fixes: sparse prefill in FULL CUDA graphs (#59986), prefill memory budgeting (#63047), MTP embedding under PP (#65816), DeepSeek-V3.2 PP (#59961).
  • GLM
    • GLM-5.3-Flash: DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE (#60895), adaptive verification (#60229), row-strided QKV into FlashKDA (#61614).
    • GLM-5.3 FP8 MoE sorted-A TMA on H200, 6.0–7.6% E2E throughput (#64760).
    • FP8 KV cache for DSpark and DFlash drafts (#63841, #64612, #65553).
    • FP32 indexer MQA logits restored for GLM-5/GLM-5.3/HY-V4, with new --attention-config.indexer_logits_dtype (#64580).
    • Fused KDA convs fix stale weights after RL refit (#60991).
  • Muse Spark
    • Opt-in Muse Spark Open specialized decode on GB300 (#64077).
    • One RoPE cache shared across layers: 11.5 GiB per GPU saved, 14.5% more KV cache on 8×B200 (#65206).
    • GEMM and communication+norm fusions (#65438, #64638); hybrid DeepGEMM MegaMoE / TRT-LLM for NVFP4 (#64525).
    • CUDA routing kernel (#64553), MegaMoE JIT warmup (#63920), DSpark draft loading fix (#65125).
  • MiniMax-M3 / M3.1
    • Sequence parallelism and GEMM-RS for TP + MegaMoE, 14–20% lower P50 TTFT (#64659), also with PP (#65537).
    • Fused norm + MXFP8 quant, 1.39–1.60× (#64852).
    • Triton query-tiled sparse prefill on Hopper (#57420); SM90 split-K indexer (#64037).
    • No host sync in prefill metadata (#65883); NVFP4 MegaMoE warmup (#66227); fmha_sm100 indexer updates (#66228).
    • Fixes: M3.1 prefill workspace (#64856), sequence parallelism (#65496), encoder CUDA graphs (#65226).
  • Kimi
    • Opt-in --attention-backend KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA for agentic workloads on Blackwell (#63638).
    • Kimi-K3 MegaMoE symmetric buffer 10.73 → 2.50 GiB per GPU at TP8 EP (#63541).
    • FlashInfer fused FP8 chunked-context K/V pack (#61527).
    • Fixes: KDA prefill OOM (#63989), NaNs via FlashKDA/FlashMLA pins (#64759), sleep mode (#64583, #66273).
    • Kimi K3.1 groundwork landed (#66030, #66028), but K3.1 is not servable in this release.
  • Qwen
    • Qwen3.5: breakable CUDA graphs instead of torch.compile (#51012); fused norm/gate + quant (#64509) and AR + norm + quant (#64723); GDN in_proj overlap (#64425, #64999).
    • GDN prefill state gather/scatter fused for Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5 and Kimi KDA, 1.16–1.50× (#66064).
    • Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: PLE disk offload via --engram-config '{"disk_offload": true}' (27 GiB less on DGX Spark, #59958), PP (#60234), shared QSA top-k buffer (#65619), loading fixes (#62318, #65812, #64820, #60490).
    • Fixes: long-context int32 overflow (#63761), multi-layer MTP (#62111).
  • Other models
    • Step5 MegaMoE with PP (#65504) and KV block sizing (#65153).
    • Gemma 4: multimodal encoder DP (#60314), PP (#65989), FA4 FP8 MMA on SM90 (#60372).
    • Moved to the Transformers modeling backend: OLMoE (#63384), Gemma v1 and StableLM (#66393), Aria (#59767; temporarily about 11% less KV cache and 25% lower image throughput).
    • Matryoshka dimensions for EmbeddingGemma 2 (#64885, #60978); RADIO C-RADIO v2/v3/v4 (#58468).
    • Qwen3-ASR on the upstream Transformers config; no --hf-overrides needed for the ForceAligner (#66097, #63274).
    • Fixes: GPT-OSS MXFP4 LoRA (#65825), PLaMo3 GPTQ (#62836), Ling3 (#65088), DomynEdge (#66819).
  • Multimodal
    • Encoder CUDA graphs for Pixtral/Mistral3 (#56277), shared capture buffers (#65084), one replay per batch up to encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget (#65227).
    • On-device input normalization for Nemotron VL (#57924), Gemma 3 (#64487), Gemma 4 (#65577).
    • --mm-encoder-tp-mode data for MiMo-V2.6 (#64179).
    • Fixes: FlashInfer ViT attention on GLM-4.1V/GLM-OCR/GLM-5.3-Flash (#65778), Qwen3-Omni and Qwen2.5-Omni video budgets (#66017, #66190), dots_ocr with TP (#64543), embedding-only startup (#65689), media cache eviction (#65363).
Engine core
  • Extensible KV cache
    • On by default on CUDA and ROCm (#56492).
    • Headroom for measured allocator fragmentation, validated on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 at TP8+EP on 8×H200 (#67296).
    • Fixes: sizing and startup OOMs (#67485, #66523, #66731, #66197, #65554), connectors that failed to start (#65225), up to 84% undersized caches on DGX Spark (#65413), --max-model-len auto (#65463).
    • Startup warning when an explicit gpu_memory_utilization withholds memory from it (#66704); docs on when to set it (#67071).
  • Model Runner V2
    • The only runner after MRV1's removal (#63373); DBO with spec decode and DCP (#61464).
    • Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes (#63406).
    • Staged writes copied straight into UVA (#63633); idle sampler writes skipped, about 10–11% faster small-batch decode (#62748).
    • Sampler warmed up after graph capture to stop memory growth under load (#62560).
    • Lower peak memory for chunked prompt logprobs (#64841, #64914); Triton ReplaySSM (#65033).
    • NVIDIA Confidential Computing decode fixes (#59981).
  • Speculative decoding
    • Suffix decoding (#60339) and custom speculators (#63205) on MRV2; draft-model CUDA graphs (#60989).
    • XPress with adaptive verification (#65175); adaptive verification draft budgets on a Triton kernel (#63421).
    • Batch-sharded draft logits (#63554); DSpark sequential blocks (#63886).
    • DSpark sliding-window MLA draft layers (#63795) under DCP (#63796); fused Markov sampling, 42–50% less sampling time (#64476); draft_lm_head_quantization (#64368).
    • Draft KV cache dtype aligned with the target (#65198).
    • Trace replay with ngram/EAGLE3/MTP, 1.47–2.03× (#63275); 3× faster resample kernel (#65100).
    • Fixes: DFlash acceptance of 0 with FULL CUDA graphs (#64059), a resample race (#66048), acceptance-estimator cancellation (#65229), standalone draft prefill under FULL graphs (#65804), grammar-invalid drafts (#61557).
  • Scheduler and engine overhead
    • Prompt token ids kept as int32 buffers: 40× less per-request CPU on a 128K prompt (#62702).
    • Per-request id lists kept out of the cyclic GC (#65300); 45–50% less KV block allocation CPU (#65831).
    • New requests and aborts handled while waiting for model output (#65466), with a cheaper wait loop (#65773).
    • Opt-in cache-aware admission via --cache-aware-admission-window (#54625).
    • --max-num-inflight-kv-loads starts async KV loads while the batch is full (#65319), with cached reservations: 47.2 → 5.4 ms per schedule (#65285).
    • A multimodal item is no longer split by a prefix hit (#65271).
  • Startup and compile
    • No openai/fastapi imports in EngineCore and workers (#65423, #65589).
    • CUDA graph memory profile skipped when its estimate is disabled (#64622).
    • Device-neutral compile cache via VLLM_COMPILE_ON_ONE_RANK, on by default (#63247); all graph-affecting config fields hashed into compile cache keys (#65652).
    • --shuffle-safetensors-files for large EP startups (#42837).
    • BasevLLMParameter's Python __torch_function__ dropped: GLM-5.2-FP8 TTFT −6.1% on GB300 (#63785).
  • Lifecycle
    • Process checkpoint/restore over HTTP (#62570); opt-in multi-worker CUDA checkpoint sleep (#64186).
    • Best-effort NUMA binding by default; --no-numa-bind to disable (#61258).
    • Sleep mode with exact-size pinned backups, up to about 578 GiB less host memory per node on Mistral Large 4 TP8 (#64630); level 2 discards only parameters (#66010, #66165, #59994).
    • Fast Start weight-cache restarts for online FP8/MXFP8, ModelOpt CUTLASS FP8/NVFP4/block-FP8 and AWQ/GPTQ Marlin (#63672, #63754, #64119, #64182), with pluggable shared warmup-cache stores (#65168).
    • WatermarkConfig.enforce (#62966).
  • RL and weight loading
    • VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct writes checkpoint tensors straight into the live model (#64336, #64352, #65281).
    • Every load and update finishes through finalize_model_weights (#65914, #64357, #64692, #57678).
    • Load plans for weight-transfer engines (#65235); per-update NCCL source ranks for PP trainers (#62557).
    • Sparse weight patches validated in one pass, 40–48% shorter pause (#66021).
    • Offloaded KV tier survives pause/sleep (#57810); partial stacked weights rejected (#63752).
  • LoRA
    • MoE-LoRA shrink/expand kernels up to 64 tokens (#64653); embedding LoRA scaled by embed_scale (#62470).
    • Rejected: adapters on unwrapped modules (#63489), non-linear expert placement with EP (#62797).
    • Fixes: reloads with requests in flight (#64616), KV-sharing fast prefill (#61162), SEQ_CLS heads (#63286), fused MoE expand rounding (#63894), Mamba-1 (#64681).
  • Batch invariance: LFM2 ShortConv (#62367), FlashInfer FP8 bmm and W4A16 NVFP4 (#62192), GPTQ (#60479), FA sliding window (#65627), aten::mm out_dtype overloads (#60047).
Large-scale serving
  • Expert parallelism and fault tolerance
    • DP+EP scale-down via POST /v1/fault_tolerance/apply (#46370); MoRI EPv2 (#61361).
    • Opt-in symm_mem EPLB weight-migration backend (#62009).
    • --enable-ep-weight-filter with EPLB: DeepSeek-R1 NVFP4 DEP8 reads 105 GiB per rank instead of 385 GiB (#64187).
    • num_redundant_experts defaults to the minimum valid value (#30614).
    • Skipped combine staging copy in flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided (#65498); DeepEP V2 padded rows (#54109).
  • Context parallelism and sparse attention
    • Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (#63956); DCP on the FlashMLA sparse bf16 KV path (#61609).
    • MLA decode up-projected before the A2A merge with --dcp-comm-backend a2a (#64994); faster DCP sparse-indexer top-k (#65178, #64129).
    • Cross-layer KV cache sharing for MLA layers (#64095).
    • Fixes: PP rank derivation under PCP (#65539), FlashInfer MLA DCP decode (#59392).
  • KV connectors
    • NIXL: push mode via transfer_mode (#64230); ucx_backend_params (rocm_ipc on MI355X: 3.4 → 483.7 Gbps, #62905); 38% fewer hybrid SSM transfer bytes (#62317); block pairing across different P/D block sizes (#59746), with mismatched push handshakes rejected (#59747); same-host NVLink with the extensible KV cache (#65137).
    • Mooncake: selective leases (#63420), automatic cache_prefix (#65160), per-GPU RDMA devices (#65076), heterogeneous-TP hybrid sharing (#54307), sleep mode (#59934), lease renewal (#64193).
    • Lookahead block hashes in NIXL, Mooncake and offloading connectors (#64096); UMBP standalone mode (#61795, #61793).
    • Out-of-tree and LMCache MP connectors with the extensible KV cache (#66605, #66674).
  • KV offload
    • SimpleCPUOffload with one host buffer per rank and opt-in HugeTLB pages (#60130); no zero-filled pool (#64345).
    • KVCR v0.2.0 (#64224, #63889); async lookups published per request group (#57474); secondary tiers rejected on multi-node engines (#62930).
    • Hardened P2P tier (#63781, #64250, #64256, #64251, #64501, #63618, #64300, #63988) and correctness fixes (#64229, #63566, #65279, #65631, #64400, #63937, #65640).
  • HiSparse
    • Uses the extensible KV cache by default: 16% more GPU+host KV capacity (#65214).
    • Fused slot invalidation, up to 1.8% lower TPOT on GLM-5.3-NVFP4 (#60103); fewer hash probes (#61263); speculative-group prefetch (#63801).
    • Platform backend for hardware plugins (#62592); scheduler deadlock fix (#62979).
  • EPD and distributed
    • Metadata-only image and video inputs for GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1 (#64071, #62802).
    • Bitwise-identical 1-stage and 2-stage custom all-reduce (#57042); FlashInfer all-reduce gated on 16-byte rows (#63123).
    • Cross-node MNNVL groups kept off CUDA IPC all-reduce (#55835).
Hardware
  • NVIDIA
    • Step5 NVFP4 TRTLLM-Gen MoE (#65152).
    • DeepSeek-V4.1: latency_specialized decode extended, 5.9–17% faster decode step on GB300 (#63921); swap-AB CuTe DSL decode attention for TP2/TP4, 1.4–2.15× (#62633); opt-in fused DSpark Markov sampling, 1.6–3.9× (#64442).
    • Sparse-indexer top-k reads BF16 logits directly (#62172, #64138); single-launch fused prefill top-k (#60618).
    • GLM-5.3 TMA MoE projections on H200 and SM100 (#63820, #65746); SM90 native small-head sparse FlashMLA, +10% on GLM-5.3-Flash TP4 (#64510).
    • CuTe DSL BF16x3 router GEMM for fp32 routers on Hopper (#61903); fused GDN MTP decode for DSpark K=8, +18% on B300 (#65874).
    • GLM-5.3-Flash on 2× DGX Spark, 15% lower TPOT (#62956); faster weight loading on integrated GPUs (#58868).
    • Rubin locality-domain NVFP4 MoE (#61685); Jetson Thor (SM110) fixes (#62133, #65050, #62275).
  • AMD ROCm
    • ROCm 10.0 only (#61939); AITER v0.1.28.post1 (#63774, #65937); MoRI EPv2 (#61361).
    • MonoKernel decode for Muse Spark Open DSpark verify (#63440), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at TP8 (#64101) and the MiniMax-M3.1 DSpark drafter, +10% P90 interactivity (#65386).
    • Kimi-K3 specialized decode (#61435), AITER-tuned prefill GEMMs: mean TTFT 5.35 → 4.05 s (#63730), opt-in FlyDSL FP8 MLA prefill (#59124).
    • DeepSeek-V4-Pro P/D over MoRIIO (#48989); Step-5-Preview (#61837) and Reflection Beam 1.0 (#62057) on ROCm.
    • RDNA: TRITON_ATTN by default (#60418), AITER Triton kernels on RDNA3 (#52970), HIP GDN prefill backend for gfx1151 (#56307), opt-in W4A16 dense prefill cache: TTFT −22 to −26% on Strix Halo (#60710).
    • Fixes: Kimi-K2.6 int4 prefill regression on Triton 3.8 (#62565), MI355 extensible KV cache OOMs (#65418).
  • Intel XPU
    • PyTorch 2.15 (#63977) and vllm_xpu_kernels 0.1.17 with new MoE/MLA interfaces (#60609).
    • Per-token dynamic FP8 activations (#61362); faster batched Triton MoE (#51605); MRoPE kernel (#59938); GDN metadata reuse (#64479); DeepSeek-V4 adaptive verification (#62309).
  • CPU
    • MRV2 on CPU backends without Triton: Arm, IBM Z, PowerPC, RISC-V (#61995).
    • zentorch 2.14.0.2 (#65669) and Laguna MoE on Zen (#63711).
    • Faster GDN spec-decode updates (#64829); Gemma 4 MoE gelu_tanh (#61593); bidirectional encoder-only attention (#63738).
  • Other: out-of-tree layer overrides via vllm.model_executor.hw_agnostic.resolve (#60218); shared routed-expert row restorers (#64689); Ascend Triton fix (#64013).
Quantization
  • New --quantization lut_b_moe: about 3.14-bit MoE experts with MXFP8 activations, native on Rubin (#62759).
  • w4afp8 checkpoints on the W4A8 FP8 MoE path (#64410).
  • Block Hadamard input rotation with online mxfp4_hadamard32 and Quark online-rotation checkpoints (#62750).
  • CSF-compressed NVFP4 block scales in ModelOpt (#64312); activation quant overrides for online MXFP4 (#51808).
  • DeepSeek-V4.1 MXFP8 linears on cuBLASLt (#64815); 3× faster MXFP4 activation quant (#63101); faster FP8 quant on SM100+ (#61641).
  • QuIP NVFP4 on Humming (#65230).
  • Fixes: NVFP4 NaN logits (#63382, #61755), Humming FP8 (#60163, #56606), hadacore (#63514).
API and frontend
  • New endpoints and options
    • /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status, /checkpoint/restore (#62570).
    • thinking_token_budget on /v1/responses (#63896); /v1/completions in vllm run-batch (#64097).
    • Streaming derender on /inference/v1/generate (#63103).
    • Anthropic Messages API: min_tokens (#65459) and thinking.type=between_tools (#65954).
    • vllm:request_render_duration_seconds histogram (#60213).
  • Tool calling and reasoning
    • New granite_toolcall_parser for Granite 4.2 (#65216); llama3_json moved to the ParserEngine (#63569).
    • Incremental streaming for Kimi K3 (#62203), tool_choice="required" (#60882), DeepSeek V4/V3.2 (#58780), GLM-4.7 (#64535), Qwen3 (#64675).
    • Fixes: DeepSeek V4.1 (#62517, #64971, #62729, #62647), GLM-4.7 (#64615), Step3 (#65274), FunctionGemma (#63992), union/enum string parameters (#64518).
  • Behavior
    • Corrupt or oversized images and disabled local media return 400 instead of 500 (#63433, #60308, #64032).
    • Responses accepts incomplete assistant/reasoning history, e.g. from Codex (#35508).
    • Multi-template processors use the default template (#63606); an empty tools array is accepted like OpenAI (#65547).

  • Model Runner V1 removed (#63373).
    • VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER and VllmConfig.use_v2_model_runner are gone; setting the env var to anything but 1 fails at startup.

    • Deprecated: parallel_drafting, capture_torch_profiler, enable_layerwise_nvtx_tracing.
  • Default --block-size is 64 instead of 16 (#63231). Backends with a preferred block size still override it (ROCm paged attention keeps 16), and an explicit --block-size still wins.
  • gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 when unset with the extensible KV cache on (#56492). An explicit value in (0.8, 1.0) that withholds 1 GiB or more logs a warning (#66704).
  • ROCm 7.2 wheels and -rocm72 images are no longer published (#61939).
  • Removed:
    • QuTLASS and the fp_quant method (#65230).
    • Marlin INT8/FP8-activation (W4A8) paths and VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE; use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG (#65542).

  • Model and plugin code: all process_weights_after_loading hooks share one signature and the loader runs every module's hook (#57678); config compute_hash() replaced by compile_factors() / hash_config() (#65652).
  • API behavior:
    • llama3_json no longer streams tool arguments incrementally (#63569).
    • Canary transcription without language returns 400 (#65445).
    • An empty tools array is accepted in both frontends (#65547, #65854).
    • /v1/systemone rejects request-supplied chat templates without --trust-request-chat-template (#64503).

  • New defaults:

items.title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

items.title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents
items.summary: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.

items.title: ToolGraph as a Q-Function for Test-Time Scaling of Tool-Use Agents
items.summary: Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.

items.summary:
Release: llm 0.37.3

A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code.

Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

Returns this:

{"a":[1]}

But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

{"a":"[1]"}

According to D. Richard Hipp:

That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

The workaround looks like this:

select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

items.story_key: story|title:nvidia dgx spark developer kit turns a desk into a supercomputing lab
items.content_excerpt: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. items.title: Goal Engineering
items.summary: The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:goal engineering
items.content_excerpt: The scope of tasks that agents can take on has increased drastically over the past few years. They have gone from simple text generation to tool calling and decision making to executing full tasks. The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Launches like that of Hone give us a glimpse into that future. In this world, designing the scope of agents is crucial. Point them in the wrong direction, and you’ll get a lot of wasted tokens. A key part of the Hone agent set up is defining metrics for them to optimize. As we’ve worked on similar styles of agents, we’ve realized something about designing the scope for agents: you want to design the scope of an agent such that it makes it as easy as possible to give feedback as the agent operates within that scope. When agents mess up, a big reason they mess up is lack of right context. In order to fix this, you need to give the agent the right context. There are different types of context. Some types of context are things like access to the right documents or APIs - that is relatively easy to fix. The trickiest context to give the agent is context that is not written down anywhere already. This context needs to be given to the agent as feedback from a human expert. This is especially important as agents expand beyond doing verifiable tasks and start taking on subjective work alongside humans within an organization. For example, if you want an agent to help optimize a business metric (like improving your ads to optimize marketing performance), there are so many nuances beyond just factual context that you want to govern how the agent behaves. You probably have a certain taste around what sounds and looks good. You have opinions about how provocative or out-there your brand can be. An agent that can’t effectively get feedback to learn these things quickly becomes useless. If the scope of your agent makes it really easy to give lots of high quality feedback on the agent’s work, that will help you immensely in building an agent that can reliably pursue a long-horizon goal. A related learning is that you want to invest a lot in an intuitive and delightful UX for reviewing agent work. The bottleneck for agents performing is often them learning from feedback. Therefore, you should seek to optimize ease and quality of feedback collection! Investing in a clear UX for that is a worthwhile investment. items.title: VIVID: A Visual Harness for Agentic Video Editing
items.summary: Video editing requires agents to make editing decisions grounded in audiovisual observations and precise temporal localization, and to evaluate their effects in rendered outputs. General-purpose coding agents possess strong comprehension, reasoning, and code execution capabilities, while media interaction and evidence management mechanisms tailored to video tasks can further unlock their editing potential. We introduce VIVID, a visual harness that supports multiple native coding agents in video post-production without additional model training. VIVID provides tools for on-demand video inspection, audio analysis, and transcription, and preserves observations alongside their corresponding media versions and temporal coordinates. Agents can actively retrieve these observations as they reason, perform edits using their native coding and shell tools, and inspect rendered outputs to guide subsequent revisions. On AgenticVBench, comprising 100 tasks across Assembly, Repair, Sequencing, and Repurpose, Codex with VIVID achieves an average score of 58.6%, an improvement of 20.2 percentage points over native Codex. items.title: Calibrate Once, Grow the Vocabulary: Candidate-Independent Scores for Conformal Risk Control in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation
items.summary: Open-vocabulary segmenters accept class names at inference. Conformal risk control can bound how often their prediction sets miss the true label, but we show that this bound breaks when names are added after calibration. On ADE20K, a threshold calibrated for 10% risk at 150 names reaches up to 15.4% risk at 845 names in released CAT-Seg models. The risk exceeds the target on every calibration split, yet the prediction sets grow far less than the target requires. In SED they instead grow larger than needed. The cause is that pruning, cross-label attention and vocabulary normalisation make each label's score depend on the other requested labels. Scores can move either way, so a threshold recalibrated at a larger vocabulary need not hold at smaller ones. We remove this dependence without training by scoring each label against a fixed reference bank of names. A label's score then stays the same when names are added, so one calibration keeps its guarantee as the vocabulary grows. The guarantee holds whatever names are added, even ones chosen per image after seeing it. On three benchmarks and five segmenters, the converted models meet the target at every vocabulary size we evaluate. For CAT-Seg and SED at alpha=10%, they use at most one more label per pixel than the released models recalibrated at the grown vocabulary. Treating names instead of images as calibration samples also bounds the miss rate of added names. If the annotated names are a random sample of the names in the calibration images, an added name's expected miss rate on those images is at most the target. For harder added names, the excess is at most their gap in mean miss rate. Applied to Grounding DINO, which splits large vocabularies into chunks, the conversion also makes inference about six times faster.

items.content_excerpt: Run and fine-tune tabular foundation models using fully managed, on-demand GPUs integrated with your Databricks data and ML workflows. by Marc Susagna Holgado , Javier Poveda Panter , Puneet Jain and Ryuta Yoshimatsu Many of the most valuable predictive machine learning applications rely on tabular data. From credit risk and customer churn to demand forecasting and predictive maintenance, these use cases have traditionally required teams to develop, train and maintain models for each prediction task. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer another approach: pretrained models that can make predictions on new datasets without task-specific training. Productionizing ML systems at scale remains a challenge for many enterprises for the following reasons: Recently, agentic solutions have helped accelerate these expensive operations, but they still rely on a bespoke-trained model for each ML task or dataset. To remove this dependency, pioneering research labs have applied the transformer architecture to tabular data at scale, creating a new category of models called Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs). Because TFMs come pretrained, they require no training on your dataset, meaning bespoke training and retraining pipelines largely disappear. Despite the impressive accuracy these models demonstrate on public benchmarks, they have not yet cracked into the mainstream of enterprise AI. This is partially due to the nascent nature of the field, as not many practitioners know about them yet, but also due to compute infrastructure requirements. In this article, we'll examine how TFMs work, compare recent models and explain the trade-offs involved in adopting them for enterprise ML. We'll then demonstrate how Databricks AI Runtime supports TFM experimentation and fine-tuning with managed GPU infrastructure, integrated development tools and model governance. TFMs largely eliminate the need for training and the overhead of maintaining bespoke models. They are pretrained on millions of diverse synthetic datasets so that they can infer relationships between variables in an unseen dataset. At prediction time, the labeled rows are passed as context alongside the rows to predict. Attention, the core of the transformer architecture, then relates each new row to those examples. items.summary: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:encoder disaggregation in vllm scaling multimodal serving with epd
items.content_excerpt: Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's inference deployment Q&A describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since our December 2025 architecture post , and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: The EPD tracker links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through #62802 . The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. EPD supports two deployment patterns: E+PD , with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and E/P/D , with all three stages deployed separately. Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode. An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings. items.content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements , then clone the repository , install dependencies, and start the engine: The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically. Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
